ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The large figure on the left is a polyomino composed of unit squares. Counting from top to bottom, it has 5 rows: rows 1, 2, and 3 each have 4 squares, and rows 4 and 5 each have 5 squares, so the total number of squares is 4+4+4+5+5=22. On the right, two kinds of small pieces are given: the upper one is a 3-square L-shaped piece, and the lower one is a 4-square one-sided L-shaped piece; the problem states that these small pieces can be rotated, but cannot be flipped. Reasoning: Let the number of needed 3-square small pieces be t, and the number of 4-square small pieces be q. The area must satisfy 3t+4q=22. Taking modulo 4, 3t≡22≡2 (mod 4), that is -t≡2 (mod 4), so t≡2 (mod 4). Therefore, if it can be tiled, the smallest possible value of t is 2. Below gives a tiling using 2 3-square pieces to show feasibility. Label the rows of the large figure on the left from top to bottom as 1 to 5, and the columns from left to right as 1 to 5; the target squares are columns 1 to 4 of rows 1 to 3, and columns 1 to 5 of rows 4 to 5. Use 4 4-square L-shaped pieces to cover: {(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1)}, {(1,4),(2,2),(2,3),(2,4)}, {(3,1),(3,2),(3,3),(4,1)}, {(4,5),(5,3),(5,4),(5,5)}. Use 2 3-square L-shaped pieces to cover: {(3,4),(4,3),(4,4)} and {(4,2),(5,1),(5,2)}. These are all rotated forms of the small pieces shown on the right, without flipping, and they exactly cover all 22 squares. Therefore at least 2 three-square figures are needed.

Exhibit a tiling with 2 such pieces: label rows top to bottom 1–5 and columns left to right 1–5, with the target cells occupied in rows 1–3 columns 1–4 and rows 4–5 columns 1–5. Use 4-square pieces on {(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1)}, {(1,4),(2,2),(2,3),(2,4)}, {(3,1),(3,2),(3,3),(4,1)}, and {(4,5),(5,3),(5,4),(5,5)}. The available pieces are the L-shaped 3-square piece and the one-sided L-shaped 4-square piece shown on the right. Color the large figure like a checkerboard. Starting with the upper-left square black, the occupied target has 11 black and 11 white squares. Any shown 4-square L piece, in any rotation, covers 2 black and 2 white squares. Any L-shaped 3-square piece covers either 2 black and 1 white or 1 black and 2 white, so each 3-square piece changes the black-white difference by 1 in magnitude. Since the target difference is 0, the number of 3-square pieces must be even. Also, 22 is not divisible by 4, so using no 3-square pieces is impossible. Therefore at least 2 three-square pieces are needed.
